entities.summary:
Charles of Provence (845–863 CE), also known as Charles of Burgundy, was a Carolingian king and ruler of Provence and Lower Burgundy from 855 until his early death in 863. He was the son of Louis the German, King of the East Francians, and his wife, Ermengueld. Born in Verdun, Grand Duchy of Lotharingia (now France), Charles was educated by the renowned scholar Alcuin of York and served as the king's emissary to the Holy Roman Emperor Lothair I. In 855, Charles succeeded his father as king of the East Francians and later became the ruler of Provence and Lower Burgundy. He played a crucial role in the Carolingian reconquest of Aquitaine from the Visigoths, a campaign that ultimately led to the restoration of the Carolingian dynasty in France.

Charles' legacy is marked by his efforts to promote education, art, and architecture during his reign. The construction of the basilica of Saint-Pierre in Vienne, France, is attributed to his patronage. He also commissioned the creation of the Gesta Francorum, a historical text that chronicled the military campaigns of the Carolingian kings.

Charles' reign was cut short by his early death on January 29, 863. He was succeeded by his son Louis the Younger, who went on to play a significant role in the Carolingian dynasty's struggle against the Viking invasions. The death of Charles of Provence marked the beginning of a period of instability in the Carolingian Empire, which would eventually lead to the fragmentation of the empire into smaller kingdoms.

The impact of Charles of Provence' reign can still be felt today in the cultural and artistic achievements of the Carolingian Renaissance. His legacy is a testament to the enduring power of the Carolingian dynasty, which played a significant role in shaping Western civilization.
